fact_text: The Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) is a temporary employer-sponsored work visa that lets an employer sponsor a suitably skilled worker to fill a position they cannot find a suitably skilled Australian to fill. On 7 December 2024 it replaced the Temporary Skill Shortage (TSS) visa.
evidence_quote: This temporary visa lets an employer sponsor a suitably skilled worker to fill a position they can’t find a suitably skilled Australian to fill.

fact_text: To be granted a Skills in Demand visa (subclass 482) you must be nominated for a skilled position by an approved sponsor, so the visa depends on having an approved sponsoring employer and is tied to the nominated role.
evidence_quote: be nominated for a skilled position by an approved sponsor

fact_text: The Employer Nomination Scheme visa (subclass 186) is a permanent residence visa that lets skilled workers nominated by their employer live and work in Australia permanently.
evidence_quote: This visa lets skilled workers, who are nominated by their employer, live and work in Australia permanently.

fact_text: The Skilled Employer Sponsored Regional (Provisional) visa (subclass 494) is a regional employer-sponsored provisional visa; holders can apply for permanent residence after 3 years from the time the visa is granted.
evidence_quote: You can apply for permanent residence after 3 years from the time we grant your visa.

fact_text: A subclass 494 (regional) visa holder can live, work and study only in designated regional areas of Australia — the major cities excluded from the regional definition are not permitted.
evidence_quote: You can live, work and study only in designated regional areas of Australia

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: a work visa lets you live anywhere in Australia. Actually: the subclass 494 is a regional visa and holders may only live, work and study in designated regional areas. Action required: confirm the intended location (e.g. Sydney) is within a designated regional area before accepting a 494 role.

fact_text: To work in Australia a permanent migrant or temporary visitor needs a valid work rights visa from the Department of Home Affairs, linked to their passport — so a sponsored professional generally cannot start work until the relevant visa is in effect.
evidence_quote: To work in Australia, permanent migrants and temporary visitors will need a valid work rights visa (from the Department of Home Affairs) which is linked to your passport or travel document.

fact_text: Once you are in Australia and hold a valid work rights visa, you apply for a Tax File Number (TFN) online through the ATO's Individual Auto-Registration (IAR) system.
evidence_quote: If you have a valid work rights visa and are located in Australia, you can apply using the Individual Auto-Registration system.

fact_text: You are not legally required to have a Tax File Number (TFN), but without one your employer or financial institution must withhold tax at a higher rate — so getting a TFN early avoids emergency (higher-rate) withholding on your pay.
evidence_quote: You don’t have to have a TFN, but without one, your employer or financial institution must withhold more tax from payments they make to you.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you must have a TFN to be paid, or a TFN is just paperwork. Actually: you can be paid without a TFN, but your employer must then withhold more tax. Action required: apply for a TFN as soon as you arrive and give it to your employer to avoid higher-rate withholding.

fact_text: If you become an Australian resident for tax purposes, you must declare all income you earn in Australia and overseas — Australian tax residents are taxed on their worldwide income.
evidence_quote: If you're an Australian resident for tax purposes, you must declare all income you've earned in Australia and overseas.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: Australia only taxes income earned in Australia. Actually: once you are an Australian resident for tax purposes you must declare worldwide income. Action required: plan for the Australian tax treatment of foreign income and assets before or soon after arrival.

fact_text: Tax residency is worked out by the ATO under its own statutory tests (resides, domicile, 183-day, and Commonwealth superannuation tests) and is separate from your immigration status — you can be an Australian resident for tax purposes without being an Australian citizen or permanent resident.
evidence_quote: can be an Australian resident for tax purposes without being an Australian citizen or permanent resident

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: you only become an Australian 'resident' for tax once you hold PR or citizenship. Actually: the ATO uses its own residency tests, so a temporary visa holder can be an Australian tax resident. Action required: work out your tax residency separately from your visa status.

fact_text: Superannuation is a compulsory employer contribution paid into a super fund on top of your wages; the Super Guarantee amount your employer must pay is 12% of the qualifying (ordinary time) earnings paid to each employee for the pay period.
evidence_quote: This is 12% of the qualifying earnings you pay to each employee for the pay period.

fact_text: In most cases people who are visiting or only temporarily in Australia do not have access to Medicare and are responsible for all their hospital and medical costs; Medicare eligibility is generally restricted to people permanently residing in Australia (citizens, permanent visa holders, and in some cases PR applicants).
evidence_quote: In the majority of cases, visitors to Australia do not have access to Medicare, and are therefore responsible for all costs associated with hospital, medical and para-medical health care rendered in Australia, whether provided in a public and or private hospital setting.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: anyone living and working in Australia gets Medicare. Actually: most temporary visa holders are not eligible for Medicare and pay the full cost of care. Action required: check your Medicare eligibility and arrange health cover for your stay (see reciprocal agreements and private insurance).

fact_text: Whether a temporary visa holder can access Medicare often depends on a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement (RHCA): if you are from a country that has an RHCA with Australia, you may be eligible for medically necessary care under Medicare while you are here.
evidence_quote: If you are from a country that Australia has a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement (RHCA) with, you may be eligible for medical care under Medicare while you are here.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: Medicare eligibility is all-or-nothing based on your visa. Actually: your home country may have a Reciprocal Health Care Agreement giving you access to medically necessary Medicare care. Action required: check whether your home country has an RHCA with Australia; Australia has agreements with 11 countries, and if yours is not one, private insurance is essential.

fact_text: If you are not eligible for Medicare you are strongly advised to hold private health insurance for your whole stay; for a number of visas holding adequate health insurance is a formal visa condition (Home Affairs lists these as visas subject to condition 8501).
evidence_quote: In the absence of Medicare eligibility, all visitors to Australia are strongly recommended to make their own arrangements for private health insurance (regardless of whether or not it is a visa condition) to ensure they are fully covered for any unplanned medical and or hospital care they may need while in Australia.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: public healthcare will cover you, or insurance is optional. Actually: without Medicare you pay full medical costs, and some visas legally require you to maintain adequate health insurance (condition 8501). Action required: take out adequate private health cover (e.g. Overseas Visitor Health Cover) before you start, and check whether your visa carries condition 8501.

fact_text: Visa holders and migrant workers have the same workplace entitlements and protections as all other employees in Australia, regardless of their migration status.
evidence_quote: Visa holders and migrant workers have the same workplace entitlements and protections as all other employees in Australia, regardless of their migration status.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed: sponsored/visa workers have weaker rights or depend entirely on their employer. Actually: visa holders have the same workplace rights as any employee regardless of migration status. Action required: if underpaid or mistreated you can seek help from the Fair Work Ombudsman; your workplace rights are the same as any other employee.
